HEADLINE: Newcrest in late surge
TEXT:
Production at Newcrest Mining has jumped in the December quarter, with year-to-date volumes for gold and copper rising on the same period last year.

In an announcement to the Australian Securities Exchange on Wednesday, the company said 655,000 ounces of gold had been produced in the December quarter, an increase of 7 per cent on the same period last year.

Copper volumes also rose, with 26,847 tonnes produced in the quarter. The result is up by 20 per cent on the prior year's December quarter which yielded 22,321 tonnes.

The $18 billion miner also said full-year production guidance for 2019 remains unchanged, however, with gold production forecast to be between 2.35 and 2.6 million ounces and copper volumes expected to reach between 100,000 and 110,000 tonnes. The preceding full year saw gold production of 2.35 million ounces and copper production of 78,000 tonnes.

Newcrest said increased production in the second half would offset lower production in the first half resulting from planned shutdown events.

The company benefited from favourable exchange rates in the December quarter. The per-unit cost measure of all-in sustaining cost, which incorporates foreign exchange rates, was $720 per ounce for the quarter, 7 per cent below the preceding three months and 13 per cent less than the December quarter in the prior year. The positive results for the miner follow suggestions late last year that the company may become a takeover target and arguments that consolidation is overdue in the sector.

HEADLINE: Vale cuts to hit iron ore
TEXT:
Iron ore markets may be hit by months of uncertain supply following Vale's announcement it will decommission a 10 further tailings dams in response to the Friday's tragic dam collapse.

Vale said on Wednesday (AEST) that 40 million tonnes of production would be taken offline as it ceased operations at mines that utilise tailings dams which the company will close as it addresses safety concerns.

CBA research analyst Vivek Dhar noted that the reduced output from Vale, if not offset, would represent a 10 per cent of the market. He said as a result the price for iron ore would likely remain high.

"Iron ore prices are likely to remain above [forecasted ranges] in the near future," Mr Dhar said. The price spike that occurred on Friday when the dam collapse news broke was just a short term response. Until Vale can reintroduce, if possible, offsetting production, it is likely the price will remain high."

The share prices of Australian iron ore miners BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue Metals rose steeply on the news. Mr Dhar said that earnings guidance for local iron ore miners may result if the commodities price remains elevated and Vale is unable to bring on offsetting supply.

Chief executive Fabio Schvartsman said Vale's board had already approved the decision to decommission the dams and suspend related mining operations.

Mr Schvartsman said those operations currently produce 40 million tonnes of iron ore and 11 million tonnes of pellets per year. Vale forecast 390 million of iron output in 2018.

The price of listed Australian iron ore miners jumped yesterday.

HEADLINE: East coast gas remains tight for buyers
TEXT:
The national competition regulator has pointed to a slightly softer outlook for east coast gas prices over the next two years based on LNG forward prices in Asia, but one producer with gas for sale says prices will still be "strong", suggesting industrial gas buyers will still have to dig deep to lock in supplies.

The latest price data for LNG "netback" prices - LNG prices less processing costs netted back to the main Queensland supply hub - released by the regulator on Wednesday suggests prices should remain within the range of about $8.20-$10.60 a gigajoule through to the end of 2020.

While the outlook points to slightly higher prices for next summer and again in late 2020 than signalled by the last release of data two weeks ago, the prices remain below the $12-$13 or more seen in 2018. The regular LNG netback data now being published by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has become an important signaller to gas buyers as to roughly what they can expect for domestic prices. But as the ACCC advises, the netback number is not the only factor driving east coast prices, while local buyers must also factor in retailing and pipeline costs.

Ian Davies, chief executive of Senex Energy, which is in talks to sell gas it expects to have available from its Atlas project in Queensland in 2020, acknowledged the transparency in the market provided by the ACCC's information but said he saw a firm outlook for local prices despite a softening in the LNG spot market in Asia.

"Prices are still strong and will remain strong because the fundamentals of gas supply aren't changing," Mr Davies said, saying Senex had attracted interest from gas buyers looking to buy more than the 13 petajoules a year that it has for sale.

He said he expected contract prices on the east coast to be "in the ballpark" of the range given by the ACCC, adjusted by as much as 20 per cent on either side depending on the firmness of delivery volumes and the flexibility allowed to the producer.

"That means eight, nine, 10, 11 dollars [a gigajoule]; I don't see that range is going to change materially," he said.

The jump-up in east coast gas prices compared to historical rates of $3.50-$4/GJ is hurting manufacturers and chemical makers, the most recent victim being western Sydney-based polystyrene cup manufacturer Remapak, which brought in administrators earlier this month.

Wood Mackenzie research analyst David Low anticipates a "tight" market prevailing in east coast gas this year and said that Senex is one of the producers well placed to benefit. He also named the major Esso/BHP joint venture in the Bass Strait, which recently gave the go-ahead for the $550 million West Barracouta project, and junior Cooper Energy, which is aiming to start commercial gas sales from its new $355 million Sole project in July. Cooper chief executive David Maxwell said recently that east coast gas buyers seem to have resigned themselves to higher prices for gas of about $10 a gigajoule, and echoed a widely held view that proposed LNG import terminals on the south-east coast would only cap - rather than reduce - domestic prices.

Several other energy juniors are seeking to tap opportunities presented by the tight east coast market. They include Leigh Creek Energy, which invited expressions of interest for the sale of up to 50 petajoules of gas despite its coal gasification project in South Australia still being at a pilot stage.

HEADLINE: Franking crackdown would penalise SMSFs
TEXT:
Big four accounting firm EY is warning clients with self-managed super funds they face being unfairly penalised by Labor's crackdown on franking credits and could be better off joining an industry fund.

EY private clients partner Ian Burgess said the plan to end dividend imputation for franking credits, worth $11 billion over two years, would hurt the savings of Australians with self-managed superannuation savings.

"Removing cash refunds on dividend imputation credits will unfairly penalise SMSF members and drive them to industry super funds," he said.

"A self-funded retiree with a significant SMSF Australian equity portfolio is seriously going to have to consider transferring to an industry super fund. We're flagging this with clients."

EY outlined a scenario in which a self-managed fund holder is now eligible for a refund on franking credits and has about $1.5 million in assets, including $1 million held in an Australian equity portfolio and $500,000 in fixed-interest products such as bonds

All of the self-funded retiree's earnings are currently tax-exempt and they make about $21,000 in refunds, calculated from a 5 per cent franked return on the portfolio.

Under Labor's proposals the self-managed fund would not receive a refund. If the retiree moved to an industry fund and commenced an income stream, the $21,000 would be received as a credit to their super account, because most industry funds have net taxable income.

While the industry fund would not be eligible for a refund of imputation credits, the credits could help reduce other tax liabilities, enabling the fund to credit members who invest in Australian share options with the benefit of the franking credits.

RSM Financial Services Australia director Evan Tsipas warned that Labor's planned changes, combined with planned changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, could heighten the risk of a recession.

"RSM estimates, based on Australian Taxation Office and CLASS data, that there are well over 600,000 SMSFs who may lose at least $5000 on average in franking refunds," he said.

"For SMSFs with no property, the average may be more than $8000 per annum or higher. Despite many critics' opinions, SMSF investors aren't necessarily wealthy."

A parliamentary hearing in Brisbane on Wednesday heard the franking credit plan would affect more than just retirees, potentially creating a bigger political headache for Labor leader Bill Shorten.

Brisbane resident Brad, who earns $70,000 a year and has two children with special needs, said he would lose $14,000 a year under the planned changes.

"This is a callous policy. It doesn't just affect retirees. This is a legitimate refund," he said.

Simon Jeffery, a construction industry professional, said a number of long-term decisions rested on unknown details of the policy.

"Do I transfer out of an SMSF into industry fund? But to do that you have to understand if the industry funds are going to be better off, and we don't know enough about the details," he said.

Mr Jeffery said he had spent time speaking to an industry super fund about the issue but the only response he received was that the fund did not know enough at this stage to provide any assistance.

Retiree David Warner argued the laws should be grandfathered and said his only option would be to use up capital if the laws went ahead.

"We will be forced to use up our capital and forced on to the pension sooner," he said.

"They should at least grandfather the provisions."

HEADLINE: Power price forecasts near 2017 levels
TEXT:
Forward prices for electricity on the wholesale market have climbed back up to levels not seen since late 2017, posing a hurdle for federal Energy Minister Angus Taylor's push to cut household power bills.

The trend is keeping energy retailers on their toes, especially after last week's once-in-a-decade run of maximum prices in both Victoria and South Australia and the re-emergence of potential shortages of generation as the mercury rises again late this week.

On Wednesday the market operator again advised of a looming shortfall in reserve generating capacity on Thursday, this time in NSW, which has been hit by unexpected outages at coal and gas power stations.

However, a similar shortfall flagged for Wednesday didn't eventuate as generators responded to the advice from the Australian Energy Market Operator, while forecasts for wholesale prices to shoot up close to the maximum of $14,500 a megawatt-hour in NSW in the afternoon also didn't materialise. A combination of climbing temperatures and outages at two coal-fired power stations in NSW - AGL Energy's Liddell and Origin Energy's Eraring - reduced levels of generating capacity available.

However, Origin reported early on Wednesday afternoon it had restarted Eraring and an AEMO spokeswoman signalled that other capacity was also expected to bid into the market to avoid any actual shortages on Thursday.

Matt Howell, chief executive of Tomago Aluminium, NSW's largest electricity consumer and the most vulnerable to any power cutbacks, said he had "no concerns" at that point of any risk to electricity supply to the smelter.

Meanwhile, sources point to the widespread drought and continuing high gas prices as two key factors contributing to the strengthening in the forward curve over the past six months. Even so, forecast prices for 2020 still remain below what was envisaged in early 2017 when the market was dealing with the relatively short-notice closure of Engie's huge Hazelwood plant in Victoria.

The Victorian baseload futures price for 2020 on the Australian Securities Exchange has surged more than 40 per cent since June 2018 and is now at about $87 a megawatt-hour, though still down on this year's $117.01/MWh. The NSW contract has jumped about 35 per cent since July to about $80/MWh while Queensland is up about 30 per cent.

Still, Mr Taylor expected electricity retailers to reduce prices to customers, despite the wholesale price situation. "It is time for the energy companies to provide a fair deal for all Australians. That's their responsibility," he said.

Prices for 2019 are higher, with both Victoria's and South Australia's base futures prices standing at more than $110/MWh.

"We were looking at the ASX electricity forward curve on electricity prices three or four months ago and it was showing a definite dip, but now that's gone," said Peter O'Connell, chief executive of Amaysim, which owns the Click Energy business.

"Everybody in the trading industry was saying we should start to see a drop off but we're not, we're seeing the reverse."

Longer term, the futures market signals prices should decline, at least in 2021, when prices are down on 2020 levels before they edge up again in 2022 when Liddell is due to close.

The Australian Energy Market Commission in December said electricity prices should fall for the next two years due to a "huge" pipeline of new renewable generation and "relatively flat" demand. But the market is volatile, with the December 2018 quarter seeing instances of wholesale prices above $100 a megawatt-hour rising to a level last seen "when volatility was elevated with the closure of Hazelwood", Macquarie Wealth Management said in a report.

It pointed to more than 800 hours in both of Victoria and South Australia when prices topped $100/MWh last quarter.

Key pointsPrices trend is keeping energy retailers on their toes as mercury rises.

Shortfall looms following unexpected coal and gas station outages.

HEADLINE: Alex Malley loses life membership
TEXT:
Exclusive | The new guard at CPA Australia is stripping former head Alex Malley and three former presidents of their life memberships of the accountants' union. The four will now have to pay the annual CPA dues coughed up by regular members.

HEADLINE: China to seek deal despite Huawei anger
TEXT:
Shanghai | China will push ahead with high-level trade negotiations in Washington this week to avert an economically crippling trade war with the United States despite outrage at criminal allegations levelled against telecoms giant Huawei.

While US-China rivalry now threatens to blow up into a technological trade war, there was no indication from Beijing on Wednesday it would abandon the next crucial round of trade talks as it sought to buoy confidence in the country's slowing economy, where 1.4 billion people have begun Chinese New Year holidays.

Chinese officials, state-controlled media and academics said Beijing would pursue a peaceful resolution to the trade dispute, with China's top economic policymaker Liu He due to meet Donald Trump on Thursday.

But there are growing fears that tensions over the proposed extradition of senior Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou and US criminal charges filed this week accusing Huawei of stealing American technology and evading sanctions against Iran would escalate into a long-term technological cold war with implications for Washington's allies, including Australia.

"The Chinese of course are hopping mad now but they really need the trade agreement. At the dinner table in Buenos Aires [at G20], the Chinese already made major concessions," Willy Lam, adjunct professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong's Centre for China Studies, said.

"They need the trade deal. [President] Xi Jinping is concerned about his position within the party and concerned about what his critics may say if he doesn't have a deal with Trump. He desperately needs a deal for economic reasons and for his own position in the party. It looks like there will be an agreement."

At the Group of 20 meeting in early December, Mr Trump agreed with Mr Xi to defer a scheduled January increase in tariffs to 25 per cent, from 10 per cent, on $US200 billion ($278 billion) of Chinese goods after China agreed to buy more US goods. Both sides have until March 1 to negotiate a permanent truce.

Markets in Asia were mixed on Wednesday as investors hold their breath ahead of the talks. The Shanghai Composite Index was flat at midday.

Mr He, the Chinese Vice-Premier, is leading a delegation of China's top foreign affairs officials and economic policymakers including the country's central bank governor, which arrived in Washington on Monday. However, the announcement by the US Justice Department alleging Huawei stole intellectual property from the US overshadowed their arrival.

US intelligence and security chiefs also issued a provocative warning on Tuesday that Chinese counter-intelligence was a major threat to the US.

"The immediate importance is the trade dispute," said Chen Hong, director of the Australian Studies Centre at Shanghai's East China Normal University. "Liu He is on the ground and some kind of deal will hopefully be made. China is ready for further opening up and collaboration with the outside world."

Despite both sides' desire for a deal, China is unlikely to agree to major structural reforms requested by Washington covering state-owned enterprises, intellectual property and cyber security. Mr Xi again emphasised China's need to be "self-reliant" in a Chinese New Year address to the nation this week, which many see as a signal of China's willingness to pursue the growth of its booming tech sector whether the US opposes it or not. Mr Xi last week warned senior government officials to be prepared for unexpected political risk.

So far, the rhetoric from Beijing towards Australia's pushback against Huawei bidding for 5G telecommunications contracts has been muted. Defence Minister Christopher Pyne this week flagged more joint operations in the South China Sea to push back against Chinese aggression, but also called for greater political and economic engagement with Beijing.

HEADLINE: Brookfield's property play for Healthscope
